```{python}
#| label: setup
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasciencedojo/datasets/master/titanic.csv'
df_titanic = pd.read_csv(url)
df_titanic.head(3)
```

# Missing Value Detection and Boolean Indexing

## `notna()` / `isna()`

`notna()` returns a **Boolean Series** where `True` if each element is not missing (NaN), and `isna()` if it is not. 
A Boolean Series functions as a "row filter" itself.

```{python}
df_titanic['Embarked'].isna().sum()   # True의 합 = 결측 개수
```

## `.loc` in Series — 1 argument

Since the Series is one-dimensional, only one row selector is entered into `.loc`.

```{python}
x = df_titanic['Embarked']
x.loc[x.notna()].unique()             # 결측 제거 후 유일값
```

## `.loc[행, 열]` in DataFrame — 2 arguments

Since DataFrames are 2-dimensional, **row selectors and column selectors are specified simultaneously** with a comma.

```{python}
df_titanic.loc[df_titanic['Cabin'].notna(), 'Cabin'].head()
```

The return type varies depending on the form of the column selector.

| Column Selector | Yes | Return |
|---|---|---|
| Single string | `.loc[cond, 'Cabin']` | Series |
| List | `.loc[cond, ['Name', 'Sex']]` | DataFrame |
| Label Slice | `.loc[cond, 'Pclass':'Cabin']` | DataFrame (**Ends Included**) |
| Omit or `:` | `.loc[cond]` | All columns |

::: {.callout-important}
## Value assignment must be `.loc[행, 열] = 값`

**Chained indexing** in the form of `df['col'][cond] = 값` 
is a common cause of bugs where assignments can be applied to copies and the original is not changed. 
Specifying coordinates with a single `.loc` call is the standard pattern.
:::

```{python}
df2 = df_titanic.copy()
df2.loc[df2['Embarked'].isna(), 'Embarked'] = df2['Embarked'].mode()[0]
df2['Embarked'].isna().sum()
```

Compound conditions are combined as `&` and `|`, but **each condition is enclosed in parentheses** 
(because `&` has higher precedence than comparison operators).

```{python}
df_titanic.loc[
    (df_titanic['Sex'] == 'female') & (df_titanic['Pclass'] == 1),
    'Survived'
].mean()
```

# `apply` — Column-by-column iteration

If you use `apply(func)` in a DataFrame, the default value is `axis=0`, and **each column 
is passed sequentially to the function as a Series**. Logically, this is equivalent to iterating through columns with a for loop, but 
it automatically combines the results into a single object.

```{python}
df_titanic[['Survived', 'Pclass', 'Sex', 'Embarked']].apply(
    lambda x: x.loc[x.notna()].unique().tolist()
)
```

If the function returns a scalar, the result is a Series; if it returns an object like a list, 
it becomes a "Series whose values are lists".

::: {.callout-tip}
## `apply` + `pd.Series` = one column into multiple columns

When applying `apply` to a Series and Lambda returns **`pd.Series`**, pandas 
uses that index as a column name and **assembles the result into a DataFrame**.
:::

```{python}
df_titanic.loc[df_titanic['Cabin'].notna(), 'Cabin'].str.split(' ')\
    .explode()\
    .apply(
        lambda x: pd.Series((x[:1], x[1:]), index=['Cabin_Type', 'Cabin_No'])
    ).head()
```

Using `x[:1]` instead of `x[0]` returns an empty string without `IndexError`, 
making slicing more defensive.

Also keep in mind that if there is a vectorized alternative, that is concise and faster.

```{python}
# apply 버전:  .apply(lambda x: x.isna().sum())
df_titanic[['Age', 'Cabin', 'Embarked']].isna().sum()   # 벡터화 버전
```

# `.str` Accessor — String Batch Processing

`.str` vectorizes and applies string methods to each string element of the Series. 
When extracting elements from the result (a Series of lists) of `split`, append `.str[i]`.

```{python}
# "성, 호칭. 이름" 형식에서 호칭만 추출
title = df_titanic['Name'].str.split(', ').str[1].str.split('.').str[0]
title.value_counts().head()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `.str.split` / `.str.rsplit`'s `n` is a keyword-only argument

Pure Python strings accept positional arguments like `'A/5 21171'.rsplit(' ', 1)`, but 
the pandas `.str` accessor signature is `rsplit(pat=None, *, n=-1, expand=False)`, 
which accepts arguments following `*` as **keywords only**.

```python
s.str.rsplit(' ', 1)     # TypeError!
s.str.rsplit(' ', n=1)   # OK
```

The "3 were given" in the error message is because `self` is automatically passed as the first positional argument. 
The reason `apply(lambda x: x.rsplit(' ', 1))` works 
is that `x` inside the lambda is an **individual Python string** rather than a Series.
:::

Since `rsplit(' ', n=1)` divides only once from the right, 
the last piece (number) is preserved even in values like `'STON/O 2. 3101282'`, which have a space in the prefix.

# `explode` — Reconstruction of observation units

Standard aggregate operations cannot be used when multiple values are grouped in a single cell ("C23 C25 C27"). 
`explode` expands each element of the list into a separate row to create "one cell = one value".

```{python}
cabin_exploded = df_titanic.loc[df_titanic['Cabin'].notna(), 'Cabin']\
    .str.split(' ')\
    .explode()
cabin_exploded.loc[[27]]    # 인덱스 27: 객실 3개 → 행 3개
```

Two key properties:

1. **Indexes are duplicated** — the original row from which each expanded value came is preserved.
2. Length increases — The unit of observation changes from "passenger" to "cabin".

# `groupby` Deepening

## `level=0` — Group by index

When the basis of `groupby` is in the **index** rather than the column, use the `level` argument. 
`level=0` refers to the first layer of the index, and if it is a single index, 
it means "group as the index itself." This is a typical combination that restores the index preserved by explode 
as the group key.

```{python}
cabins_per_passenger = cabin_exploded.groupby(level=0).size()
cabins_per_passenger.value_counts()   # 객실 개수별 승객 수
```

`size()` counts the **number of rows** in the group, and `count()` counts the **number of non-missing values**.

## `agg` vs `transform`

It is the same group operation, but the **method of returning the result** is different.

| | Calculation | Return Type | Unit of Observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `agg` (`median()` etc.) | Statistics by group | Rows equal to **number of groups** | Group |
| `transform` | Statistics by group | **Same length/index as original** | Original row |

`transform` operates in three steps: split → grouped calculation → **broadcast** ( 
returning the value of its own group to each row). Conceptually, it 
is an operation that maps the conditional statistic $E[Y \mid \text{그룹}]$ to each observation.

```{python}
df3 = df_titanic.copy()

# 호칭별 나이 중앙값을 각 승객에게 대응시킨 891행 Series
age_median_by_title = df3.groupby(title)['Age'].transform('median')

# .loc 대입은 인덱스 정렬 기반 → 원본과 인덱스가 같아야 결측 위치에 정확히 들어간다
df3.loc[df3['Age'].isna(), 'Age'] = age_median_by_title

print(df3['Age'].isna().sum())
print(round(df_titanic['Age'].mean(), 3), '→', round(df3['Age'].mean(), 3))
```

If the result of agg (a short Series where the index is a name) is passed to the right side, 
NaN is assigned to everything because the indices do not match. The reason `transform` is needed is this **sorting compatibility**.

Typical usage: Group-specific missing data replacement, within-group standardization 
`(x - x.mean()) / x.std()`, weight relative to group sum `x / x.sum()`.

# Summary Cheat Sheet

| Things I want to do | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Specific column of non-missing rows | `df.loc[df['c'].notna(), 'c']` |
| Assign value to missing position | `df.loc[df['c'].isna(), 'c'] = 값` |
| Column-wise iteration | `df[cols].apply(lambda x: ...)` |
| One column → Multiple columns | `s.apply(lambda x: pd.Series(..., index=[...]))` |
| Split string and extract elements | `s.str.split(p).str[i]` |
| Split once from the right | `s.str.rsplit(' ', n=1)` (`n=` required) |
| Multiple values in a single cell → Multiple rows | `s.str.split(' ').explode()` |
| Aggregate based on original row after explode | `.groupby(level=0).size()` |
| Paste group statistics into each row | `.groupby(k)['c'].transform('median')` |
